title: An Exploration of the Physiological and Psychological Aspects of Student Anxiety Using a Greenspace Restorative Environment Based on Virtual Reality: A Controlled Experiment in Nanjing College
research_question: To investigate the effects of restorative environmental components (terrain scene, pavement material, and scene green visual rate) on student anxiety from both physiological and psychological perspectives using a greenspace environment created via virtual reality.

participants.description: College students, aged 22–26 years, with a 1:1 male-to-female ratio, from Nanjing College. Participants generally believed they had mild depression, low self-rated anxiety, and good health, and did not take any drugs affecting their physical/mental state.
participants.recruitment: Invitation through online social platforms and offline publicity.

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
Five virtual greenspace scenes were presented during the recovery period, each lasting 5 minutes, with random switching between 5 observation points within scenes. Scenes varied across three components:
1.  **Terrain Scene**: Scenario 1 (with altered terrain, based on actual slope conditions) vs. Scenario 2 (flat field, no terrain modifications).
2.  **Pavement Material**: Scenario 3 (natural materials: marble, pebbles, granite, wood, plain soil) vs. Scenario 4 (artificial materials: cement, asphalt, glass, steel, concrete).
3.  **Scene Green Visual Rate**: Varied continuously (15% to 66%) and categorized into four grades: lower (<37%), low (37%–42%), high (42%–54%), and higher (>54%).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: 2.1.4. Procedure and Experimental Scene Setting, Figures 3, 4, 6

mechanisms: Tactile experiences may enhance the sense of connection with nature and aid in psychological recovery (for pavement material effect on SCL).
Dense vegetation can obstruct the view and cause discomfort or even fear; places with moderate tree cover may be more suitable for recreational activities (for green visual rate effects).
An inverted U-shaped dose–response curve for green visibility on stress recovery, indicating that 'the higher, the better' is not always true.
Nonlinear relationship between environmental elements (terrain, pavement, green visual rates) and emotions (proposed for null effects on emotions for terrain/pavement).
implementation_implications: Incorporate unrolling terrain in greenspace design to improve student anxiety.
Use natural paving materials in greenspace design to improve student anxiety.
Adjust the green amount of greenspaces to a green vision rate of 42%–54% for high recovery efficiency regarding student anxiety.
For spaces designed to attract students, aim for a greenery area of 50% green visual rate.
For spaces designed to enhance positive emotions, aim for a greenery area of 48% green visual rate.
For spaces designed to alleviate negative emotions, aim for a greenery area of 40% green visual rate.

limitations: A gap remains between VR technology and reality, requiring comparative experiments between virtual and actual experiences.
The study was based on vision only; multisensory experiences (smells, touch, taste) were not simulated due to technical reasons, limiting the ecological validity.
Subjects were limited to one university due to the COVID-19 pandemic, limiting the universality of results.

Physiological indicators may require more refined measurement and analysis methods, as they can be disrupted by several factors, making it difficult to capture the relationship between restorative benefits and greenspace components.

Limitations in experimental design and measurement methods may have led to different trends in observed results (e.g., subtle associations not observed due to insufficient experimental measurements or improper analytical methods).
Inability to perceive tactile changes in pavement material in VR.
Technical limitations of modelling software material libraries for creating more representative paving styles.
Failure to capture nonlinear relationships for terrain/pavement/green visual rate on positive emotions may lead to uncertainty in results.

The reporting of 'independent sample t-test' for comparisons where 'n=36' is stated for both groups, despite a total N of 36 participants, is inconsistent and likely a misreporting for a paired t-test.
